update_log: Comprehensive expansion of traditional Indian paintings and regional martial arts, including Pichhwai and Sqay, for Art & Culture Static GK.

indian_paintings.key_features: Created using fingers, twigs, brushes, and matchsticks with natural dyes. Characterized by eye-catching geometrical patterns and themes of Hindu deities (Rama, Krishna, Shiva).
Tribal art created mostly by women. Uses basic geometric shapes (circles, triangles, squares) to depict daily life and nature. Traditionally painted white on a red ochre background.
Traditional cloth-based scroll painting. Known for intricate details and mythological narratives, primarily revolving around Lord Jagannath and the Vaishnava sect.
Literally means 'pen work'. It is a type of hand-painted or block-printed cotton textile produced using only natural dyes. Two main styles: Srikalahasti and Machilipatnam.
Celebrated for its rich, flat, and vivid colors, simple iconic composition, and surface richness. Uniquely uses 22-carat gold foil, glass beads, and semi-precious stones.
A religious scroll painting and folk deity art. Traditionally done on a long piece of cloth (phad) to depict the epics of local deities like Pabuji and Devnarayan.
Intricate and visually stunning paintings created on cloth, typically depicting tales from Lord Krishna's life, especially as Shrinathji. Used as backdrops in temples.
Practiced by the Gond tribe. Characterized by a sense of movement created through intricate dots, lines, and dashes. Focuses heavily on flora and fauna.
Originated in the 19th century around the Kalighat Kali Temple in Kolkata. Known for bold outlines and vibrant colors, often depicting both mythological stories and satirical social commentary.
A Tibetan Buddhist painting on cotton or silk appliqué, usually depicting a Buddhist deity, scene, or mandala. Highly prominent in Himalayan states.

indian_martial_arts.key_features: Considered one of the oldest surviving martial arts in the world. Incorporates strikes, kicks, grappling, preset forms, and weaponry (swords, shields, flexible swords called Urumi).
A traditional martial art associated with the Sikh community. It is a weapon-based martial art primarily using wooden sticks to simulate swords.
Translates to 'Sword and Spear'. An armed martial art that integrates various external weapons with the internal practice of physical control through rhythmic movements.
A traditional sport in which a gymnast performs aerial yoga or gymnastic postures and wrestling grips in concert with a vertical stationary or hanging wooden pole. (State sport of MP).
A weapon-based martial art primarily using a bamboo staff (Silambam). It emphasizes footwork and the use of the staff to strike, block, and disarm opponents.
Created by Rajputs, 'Pari' means shield and 'Khanda' means sword. Its steps and techniques are widely used in the famous Chhau dance.
An armed method of martial art created by the Marathas. Particularly known for its use of the uniquely Indian patta (sword) and vita (corded lance).
An ancient, unarmed, bare-knuckle martial art from the Indian subcontinent, resembling modern kickboxing and incorporating punches, kicks, knees, and elbow strikes.
A martial art developed in Kashmir utilizing a single-edged synthetic sword paired with a shield, focusing on precise strikes and defensive maneuvers.
